title: Hello, Quarto
text:
Well, this is my first experience in blogging and using github websites. Special thanks to my brother Hyoungchul Kim for kickstarting this page. As a non-coder to the bone, I would never have pulled it off without help. Guess having a geek-Ph.D student as a brother pays off after all.
This website will have two primary purposes for me. #1 is Personal Documentation, and #2 is Linkable Online Resume. I will mostly focus on my personal blogging in #1, and my career related activities in #2. The biggest challenge will be motivating myself to keep documenting parts of my life on this website. Guess i’ll have to hope for interesting things worth writing about to come along.
What I plan for writing in #1 are Anecdotes,Reviews, and Shitposts. Categories for #2 are not determined yet; will update thoughout next year. I’ll try to keep most of my content in english, but if some posts are better off writing in korean, I will probably do so.
Thats all for this first post, lets hope it doesn’t end up being the last. Cheers!

title: Job Search in 2025
text: Getting a job in 2025 was a major pain in the ass; the job market and myself both at fault. My specific career preference for global corp dev narrowed down my applicable job openings, and the declining hire volumes reduced my chances of landing an interview. To cut it short, I ended up with 15 resume applications, 4 interview requests, and 2 final offers.

title: Job Search in 2025
text:
The Resume Grind
For my previous experience details, check out my CV in the main page
To sum up my previous intern experience, I worked as a overseas sales intern for a small medical instrument manufacturing company, an investment intern for a CVC, and a RA for a consulting firm. Melting them down to keywords would be: Global Business, SI/FI Investments, and Business Strategy. Having intern experience in Overseas sales, VC and Consulting is good and all, but its not a great fit for mass-applying in the South-Korean job market. Most job openings for juniors with business management accumulate to marketing and sales, and a rare pinch of misc job posts.
Even though marketing has the greatest amount of hire for most companies, they also require specific skill sets and portfolios to back them up. Having none of these meant that I had no competitiveness in this sector. That basically meant sayonara to the 50% of job openings for me. For sales, although I have a bit of experience, it was pretty clear to me that the culture fit between me and the sales department was a mile long. Well, there goes an another 40%. TLDR; I was going to have to fight for my chances in the 10% of all job openings. A pretty grim start.
Working with the remaining 10%, I had to find job posts that fit with my keywords. Of the three, the most generally applicable keyword was global business and business strategy. Some examples were:

Samsung Fire&Marine Insurance Global Business Development Role
Hyundai Capital Global Business Management Role
Korean Air General Hire

hire first, distribute later kind of hire

Orion Snacks Global Procurement Role
Hyundai Card Product Development Role
….. to a total of 15 applications

This total of 15 applications still included some roles like Global Marketing and Financial Accounting that I felt less competitive in. Why did I still apply? Well, #1 because I was desperate and #2 in hope to get more interview experience. Anyway, after a long wait I got 4 interview requests from these roles:

Samsung Fire&Marine Insurance Global Business Development Role
Hyundai Capital Global Business Management Role
Korean Air General Hire
Orion Snacks Global Procurement Role

A 27% win rate doesn’t really cheer you up. Especially when you have superb colleagues making 40~50% out of theirs. Anyways, time to analyze my success and failures.

Success

Samsung Fire&Marine Insurance Global Business Development Role

Global Business, SI/FI Investments, Business Strategy

Hyundai Capital Global Business Management Role

Global Business, Business Strategy

Korean Air General Hire

Global Business, Preference for SNU Undergrads

Orion Snacks Global Procurement Role

Global Business, Business Strategy




Failure

Hyundai Card Product Development Role

Business Strategy

CJ Olive Young Global Marketing

Global Business

Kakaopay Platform Business

Business Strategy

Lotte Wellfoods Global Strategy

Global Business, Business Strategy, Aversion for SNU Undergrads


In the end, it boils down to two major differences; JD Fit and Culture Fit. JD Fit being the amount of Job Experience keywords that befit the position’s JD, and Culture Fit regarding the firm’s overall qualitative tendency that could favor/dislike you. I generally got interview offers from positions with two or more befitting keywords, or firms that have strong tendencies to favor certain aspects of my qualifications. On the other hand, I had no luck from positions with weak ties with my keywords, or firms that have strong tendencies to dislike certain aspects of my qualifications. More on this matter at the Reflections and Thoughts.

title: Job Search in 2025
text:
Interviews
All interviews had different formats and number of rounds. Let me lay them out in a quick list.

Interview Format

Samsung Fire & Marine Insurance Global Business Development Role

One day interview, Offline, 2 Rounds, Presentation + In-depth format

Hyundai Capital Global Business Management Role

Interview + Internship, Online, 2 Rounds, Practical + In-depth format

Korean Air General Hire

Interview, Offline, 3 Rounds, Practical + Presentation + In-depth format

Orion Snacks Global Procurement Role

One day interview + Internship, Online, 2 Rounds, Debate + In-depth format


Most interview offers didn’t come with ideal pacing. My first interview with Orion Snacks was scheduled for Oct.31. For Hyundai/Samsung/Korean Air(2nd Round) it was Nov. 17, 18, 21 respectively. Basically I had my one and only interview testbed with Orion, and had to go through 3 interviews with very little or no intervals. Let’s go into some details of how some of the interviews went.


Orion
Using debate format, 6 applicants were divided into two and were asked to prepare pro & con arguments for a given topic. The topic was ‘Are AI created artworks truly art?’. One applicant was asked to take the additional role of moderator, which I took. The overall debate was subpar to say the least. Given the limited amount of time, it was all about securing more speaking time rather than the actual quality of arguments. Looking back, I think the debate in itself was quite unimportant and more about showing who you are in a discussion environment… but i still have doubts about how this format is suitable for that kind of assessment.
After the debate, the interviewers asked us random questions like ‘Sales pitch your elementary school’. I guess it was to determine the quickness of one’s thought processes. But as you can see, the quality of the questions were a bit… lame.
The in-depth interview with the executive staff members was conducted in a much more serious atmosphere. I received multiple challenges concerning loyalty. ‘Why not stay in the consulting business?’ was the most frequently asked question across the multiple rounds of interviews. I initially denied my interest in the consulting industry, which in hindsight was a mistake. A more truthful approach would have shown more genuineness. Also, when I was asked ‘Why did you sign up for this specific role?’ I answered with sth in the line of ‘Because I believe it is the most important role in terms of ….’. A MAJOR fuck up. I instantly realized the mistake when the executive replied ‘Just to be clear… every role is important’. A very naive answer from my part.
As a result I failed to get an internship offer, which was not a surprise. The lack of presence in the debate, wrong approach to the questions, and the educated expectation that SNU students wouldn’t stay long at the firm all added upto this result.
Key Takeaways were as follows:

Get ready for loyalty questions, and answer them with genuineness.

Denying sth obvious ends up making you look dishonest.

Refrain from answering ‘why this position’ with ‘It’s the most important role’.

To the firm, EVERY ROLE is important. These answers make you look arrogant.

It’s quite hard to convince some firms with historical data that indicate ppl like you tend to leave quick.

Do your best, but don’t sulk even if you end up rejected.




Hyundai Capital
Hyundai Capital(HC) was the only firm using online-interview format. As a person who strongly prefers face-to-face interviews, this wasn’t great. Having Samsung FMI interview the next day didn’t help either. I spent most of my time studying up on HC’s recent business issues and finantial statements.
During the interview, I was joined with 5~6 ppl. One of them was a young junior(I remember this because of what soon happens later). The general atmosphere of the interview was… monotone. It was less of a conversation and more of a interrogation. To give you a brief idea…

Q1. Why did you apply for this firm?

Because I have interest in… blahblahblah

Cool. Q2. What’s your strength and weakness?

Strength is blah and weakness is blahblah

Okay. Q3. What did you learn about in our finanacial statements?

To my understanding… blahblahblah…


Basically, there were ZERO followup questions. This meant I couldn’t appeal about my experience and what i’ve studied about the firm in detail. This probably meant that the interviewers weren’t convinced with my resume, and had less interest in me.
But then came the worst part. The junior interviewer asked me, “Could you tell me your opinion on the future of US stock market, and back it up with specific data?”.



WTF…?


Why would you randomly ask me about the US stock market? And back it up with data?? For a second I was genuinely confused and asked him what the question was lol. After a long bullshitting session, the senior next to him asked me “Great, can you repeat what you said in English?”. Well, that was the finishing blow for me.
Key Takeaways were as follows:

If the interview is getting stale, you have to make the interviewer curious.

Just repeating Q, A’s won’t get you the position. Next time, prepare something special to make the interviewer genuinely curious

Don’t include things in your resume that you can’t 100% explain.

The junior probably asked that random question because of my brief experience in quant investments. Refrain from using sources that may bring up random questions that you can’t answer well.




Samsung FMI
Samsung FMI’s global business development JD was almost a perfect fit with my prior experience. Since their role was #1 Organic Growth (managing business strategies for foreign subsidiaries) #2 Inorganic Growth (Source and evaluate investment deals), they required experience in Global Business, SI/FI Investments, Business Strategy. As a result, I had a lot to appeal in my resume and cover letters. Consequently, I also got a lot of follow-up questions about my experiences and my interest about the firm, opening up the window to showcase what I have prepared to the fullest. Also, I answered all loyalty related questions with genuineness this time which definitely had a better response from the executives. Admitting that I had once pursued a career in consulting, and then backing it up with reasons why I pivoted to this firm seemed to be the answer.
For the presentation part, it was definitely challenging material. However, they were also answerable with enough prep about the department’s recent business. Reaching out to a employee in that firm about recent issues and problems that are deemed important within the firm definitely helped in picking out the right problems to talk about. There were a lot of challenges and follow-up questions, but most of them were not too hard to answer. When asked about sth way too detailed for me to answer, admitting that I do not have enough knowledge to answer then proceeding to give the best answer you can give seems to be a good approach.
Overall, the interview felt good because the interview felt like a real conversation. It showed that the interviewers were genuinely interested about me, and I answered them with no errors.
Key Takeaways were as follows:

The ability to show your fit in the resume determines how the interview will go.

comparing to HC’s case, if you showcase well that you are fit with the position from the resume, the interviewers will provide you with opportunities to show off your skills.

Be honest, then back them up with logical reasoning.

Be honest about things that are obvious. Then add logical reasoning that explains the ‘why’

Prep as hard as you can, then search for employee’s advice.

You need to figure out what the actual employees think are the most pressing issues in the firm. Asking an actual employee is the best option. Reach out to friends, former colleagues and seniors for ties.




Korean Air
Since this blog is getting way longer than expected, i’ll cut this one short. The interview process seemed like a gimmick, since no questions seemed insightful. The general feeling was that they just wanted undergrads from prestige universities.

title: Job Search in 2025
text:
Final Offer Decisions
In the end, I got offers from Samsung FMI and Korean Air. I chose Samsung FMI over Korean Air for mainly two reasons:

Career Pathing

Samsung FMI provided a perfect fit for developing my skill set as a global business & investment professional, while Korean Air was general hire.

Salary & Location

Samsung FMI offered a much better salary plan, and a short commute route.

title: Job Search in 2025
text:
Aptitude Tests
Like most other companies worldwide, South Korean firms also require applicants to take their own aptitude tests. Some use their own, while others use 3rd party programs. Samsung uses GSAT, while most others use a test designed by Jobda. Jobda’s gamification tests and interviews are generally easy to handle. My personal take is that Jobda tests are just a very light screening tool, or just a convenient excuse for taking more time to review the applicant’s resumes.
GSAT was a totally different story. Since this test was here for a long time, there were already multiple books covering the types of questions, and time saving gimmicks. I had to ‘git gud’ in a short amount of time so that I could make it into the 3~5 multiple. It was a nightmare. Endless repetition of mock tests, pushing myself so that I could get more answers in a limited amount of time, sometimes it felt like way too much for me mentally. All I can say is… Thank God It’s Over.
